stat Machine Learning.title: Posterior contraction rates for banded approximations of Gaussian processes
stat Machine Learning.summary:
Gaussian process regression models are widely used in modern statistics and machine learning due to their flexibility, interpretability, built-in uncertainty quantification, and strong theoretical foundations. However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$.
  For large datasets commonly encountered in practice, this becomes infeasible and necessitates the use of approximate posterior methods.
  In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points.
  We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained.
  We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

stat Machine Learning.title: When Can Learned Uncertainty Be Trusted? An Audit of Distributional Reinforcement Learning
stat Machine Learning.summary: Many learned predictive models represent their uncertainty as a probability distribution, and planners and policies use this distribution to judge risk. However, the fact that a model outputs a distribution does not tell us whether that distribution captures the uncertainty in the environment which is relevant for a decision. In this work we study this question in distributional reinforcement learning, where the learned return distribution P_θ(Z | s,a) can be compared directly with an environment-grounded distribution P_env(Z | s,a) estimated by snapshot-restart Monte Carlo. Our audit first screens for the claims that a risk-sensitive user would act upon, using the excess Wasserstein gap between the top two actions (which is equal to the mass by which first-order stochastic dominance is violated). Each claim is then tested against ground truth using permutation nulls, bootstrap refutation and FDR control. Across QR-DQN, C51 and IQN on MinAtar (33 runs), 40-95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence, their placement is statistically indistinguishable from a truth-blind placement, and almost none of them can be confirmed. A similar pattern is seen for a pretrained full-Atari QR-DQN. On positive controls of known magnitude the same audit confirms 96-100% of real claims (correlation 0.89-0.92), so it is able to detect real risk when it is present. Acting on the learned CVaR advice at the most-flagged states gives results ranging from beneficial to significantly worse than chance. Ensembling, risk-sensitive training and recalibration do not fix the problem, and the recalibration experiment indicates that the learned spread has no usable information about the true risk. Based on these results, we suggest that uncertainty estimates, including those of learned world models, should be checked against realized outcomes at the decisions where they are used..
stat Machine Learning.comment: 25 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables (main text); includes supplementary material

stat Machine Learning.title: Double Machine Learning for Panel Data: Identification, Specification, and a Bank Regulation Effect
stat Machine Learning.summary: This paper examines robustness and causal interpretation of panel estimates using double/debiased machine learning. The prototype treatment setup is the 2018 US banking regulation. Under common treatment timing, we characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of specified "within" and "first-difference" scores. Simulations assess panel model transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap. Empirically, estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth. Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across four Machine Learners (ML); doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights. Both bank groups received relief, so we estimate differential exposure effects. The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification.

stat Machine Learning.title: Recursive State-Augmented Language Models: Persistent Latent-State Adaptation of Pretrained Language Models
stat Machine Learning.summary:
Language models rely on finite token contexts, limiting access to earlier interactions. We introduce Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework in which a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation. We develop deterministic and stochastic formulations.
  The experiments evaluate only deterministic SALM with frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from its decoder context. On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline, with earlier evidence available solely through a 64-dimensional state. Zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with codewords unseen in training, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance, but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule. These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.

stat Machine Learning.title: Corrected Integrated Laplace Approximation for Bayesian Inference in Latent Gaussian Models
stat Machine Learning.summary: Latent Gaussian models (LGMs) are a popular class of Bayesian hierarchical models that include Gaussian processes, as well as certain spatial models and mixed-effect models. Efficient Bayesian inference of LGMs often requires marginalizing out the latent variables. For LGMs with a non-Gaussian likelihood, exact marginalization is not possible and a popular approach is to do approximate marginalization with an integrated Laplace approximation (ILA). Using ILA produces an approximate posterior which, in some settings, can differ significantly from the correct posterior, which impacts downstream applications. We propose an importance sampling scheme to correct the error introduced by ILA. By increasing the number of samples in importance sampling, the posterior with ILA converges to the correct posterior. This idea is realized with various techniques, including pseudo-marginalization, quasi-Monte Carlo and randomized quasi-Monte Carlo. We implement our methods in an automatic differentiation framework to support gradient-based algorithms when doing inference on the hyperparameters. For the latter, we specifically consider the use of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. We demonstrate the benefits of reduced error in various applied models.
stat Machine Learning.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

stat Machine Learning.title: Distribution-First Framework for Learning Risk-Sensitive Individualized Treatment Rules
stat Machine Learning.summary: Learning a risk-sensitive individualized treatment rule (ITR) with patient covariates is challenging when the treatment criterion depends on the full conditional outcome distribution rather than only its conditional mean. Existing methods are largely criterion-specific, making it difficult to compare multiple treatment criteria within a common pipeline, such as quantiles, conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and complex preference-based objectives such as cumulative prospect theory. We propose a distribution-first framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning that first estimates treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions and then constructs the target ITR by plug-in criterion evaluation. The proposed framework unifies treatment rule learning across multiple criteria and accommodates hard-to-optimize objectives within the same estimation pipeline. On the theoretical side, it yields a general error propagation result for locally Hölder-stable criteria, linking first-stage distribution estimation error to downstream criterion estimation and treatment regret, together with sharper regret bounds under standard margin conditions. Empirically, we show that the proposed framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings and further evaluate it on the ACTG175 HIV clinical trial, a randomized study comparing several antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected adults.

stat Machine Learning.title: Pseudo-Labeling for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation with Kernel GLMs
stat Machine Learning.summary: We propose a principled framework for unsupervised domain adaptation under covariate shift in kernel Generalized Linear Models (GLMs), encompassing kernelized linear, logistic, and Poisson regression with ridge regularization. Our goal is to minimize prediction error in the target domain by leveraging labeled source data and unlabeled target data, despite differences in covariate distributions. We partition the labeled source data into two batches: one for training a family of candidate models, and the other for building an imputation model. This imputation model generates pseudo-labels for the target data, enabling robust model selection. We establish non-asymptotic excess-risk bounds that characterize adaptation performance through an "effective labeled sample size", explicitly accounting for the unknown covariate shift. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate consistent performance gains over source-only baselines.
stat Machine Learning.comment: 62 pages, 6 figures. Python solvers and experiment scripts are available at: https://github.com/nathanweill/pseudolabel-uda-experiments

stat Machine Learning.title: A Sensitivity Framework for Assessing External Validity
stat Machine Learning.summary: Assessing the external validity of experimental results is a pervasive challenge in causal inference as internally valid findings need not generalize beyond sites in which the experiments were conducted. Since the number of sites is often smaller than the number of site-level variables that moderate causal effects, we develop a partial identification framework that lets practitioners assess external validity under a wide range of assumptions that allow extrapolation across site-level variables. Our optimization-driven approach can accommodate any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as interaction terms being dominated by direct effects (the "effect hierarchy principle"). Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting---underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular---we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager (2019), whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

stat Machine Learning.title: Environment-Robust Representation Learning with Empirical Bayes
stat Machine Learning.summary: We consider multi-environment prediction problems. We assume the environments change the distribution of a latent variable, while the mechanisms generating observed covariates and targets remain stable conditional on that variable. For example, hospitals or clinical cohorts may differ in the prevalence of latent patient states, even though the relationships between those states, physiological measurements, and outcomes remain unchanged. Given a dataset from multiple environments, we formulate a Bayesian model for such problems and derive the corresponding variational objective. We show that this objective decomposes into per-environment terms and an additional cross-environment balancing term induced by the model's structure. We use an empirical Bayes method to set the prior and incorporate it into the objective. Based on this objective, we develop an amortized variational algorithm for posterior approximation, and use the resulting learned latent variables to form predictions in new environments.We study our approach through simulations and real-world studies of astronomical source identification, microbiome-based disease detection, and ICU sepsis prediction. Across these settings, our method outperforms previous approaches for prediction in new environments.

stat Machine Learning.title: Edge of Stability Selectively Shapes Learning Across the Data Distribution
stat Machine Learning.summary: Existing analyses of the edge of stability (EoS) treat it as a global property of optimization. We show that it is also selective: the stability constraint redistributes learning across subsets of the training distribution, amplifying progress on some groups while suppressing progress on others. Using a branching intervention that enters or exits the EoS regime from the same training state, we causally demonstrate this trade-off and identify two necessary conditions for a group to benefit. First, its aggregate gradient must align with the top Hessian eigenvector. We isolate this mechanism with a controlled perturbation that preserves distance but randomizes direction, destroying alignment and eliminating the advantage. Second, the group must sustain non-vanishing gradient magnitude over time. Under cross-entropy loss, gradient saturation decouples confidently classified groups, shifting the advantage to output-outliers, whose gradients persist. Together, these results show that EoS functions not only as a stability boundary, but as a mechanism governing the allocation of learning across the data distribution.

stat Machine Learning.title: Fréchet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
stat Machine Learning.summary: We propose Fréchet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fréchet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fréchet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.

stat Machine Learning.title: Calibeating Prediction-Powered Inference
stat Machine Learning.summary: We study semisupervised mean estimation with a small labeled sample, a large unlabeled sample, and a black-box prediction model whose output may be miscalibrated. A standard approach in this setting is augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) [Robins et al., 1994], which protects against prediction-model misspecification but may be inefficient when the prediction score is poorly aligned with the outcome scale. We introduce Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, which post-hoc calibrates the prediction score on the labeled sample before using it for semisupervised estimation. This simple step requires no retraining and can calibeat the original score, improving it both as a predictor of the outcome and as a regression adjustment for semisupervised inference. We study both linear and isotonic calibration. For isotonic calibration, we establish first-order optimality guarantees: isotonic post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency relative to the original score and simpler post-processing rules, while replacing the fitted isotonic score by its conditional-mean oracle yields no additional first-order variance reduction. For linear calibration, we show first-order equivalence to PPI++. We also clarify the relationship between existing estimators, showing that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization [Rubin and van der Laan, 2008]. In simulations and real-data experiments, our calibrated estimators often outperform PPI and are competitive with, or outperform, AIPW and PPI++. We provide an accompanying Python package, ppi_aipw, at https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/.
stat Machine Learning.comment: A conference version of this paper was accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Published conference version: https://openreview.net/forum?id=kh57rITtAA. Paper website: https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/

stat Machine Learning.title: Penalty-Based First-Order Methods for Bilevel Optimization with Minimax and Constrained Lower-Level Problems
stat Machine Learning.summary: We study a class of bilevel optimization problems in which both the upper- and lower-level problems have minimax structures. This setting captures a broad range of emerging applications. Despite the extensive literature on bilevel optimization and minimax optimization separately, existing methods mainly focus on bilevel optimization with lower-level minimization problems, often under strong convexity assumptions, and are not directly applicable to the minimax lower-level setting considered here. To address this gap, we develop penalty-based first-order methods for bilevel minimax optimization without requiring strong convexity of the lower-level problem. In the deterministic setting, we establish that the proposed method finds a lifted $ε$-KKT point with $\tilde{O}(ε^{-4})$ oracle complexity. We further show that bilevel problems with convex constrained lower-level minimization can be reformulated as special cases of our framework via Lagrangian duality, leading to an $\tilde{O}(ε^{-4})$ complexity bound that improves upon the existing $\tilde{O}(ε^{-7})$ result when the lower-level Slater's condition holds. Finally, we extend our approach to the stochastic setting, where only stochastic gradient oracles are available, and prove that the proposed stochastic method finds a nearly lifted $ε$-KKT point with $\tilde{O}(ε^{-9})$ oracle complexity.

stat Machine Learning.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Just Classification and a Few Regressions
stat Machine Learning.summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to recover a reward function from observed behavior, but rewards are typically only partially identified: many reward--value pairs can induce the same behavior policy. We study this problem in the maximum-entropy, or Gumbel-shock, model under a broad class of statewise affine normalization constraints, with anchor-action constraints as a special case. This leads to Generalized Policy-to-$Q$-to-Reward (GenPQR), a modular approach to normalized reward recovery based on policy estimation and $Q$-evaluation via the Bellman equation; both components can be instantiated with off-the-shelf classification and regression methods. We establish modular finite-sample guarantees under general function approximation, with separate terms for policy-estimation and $Q$-function estimation error. We also give explicit bounds for GenPQR with fitted $Q$-evaluation. In experiments, GenPQR improves on DeepPQR in reward recovery. Our guarantees extend beyond anchor actions, accommodate large action spaces, and are not tied to a specific neural-network architecture or training procedure.

stat Machine Learning.title: Gradient Flows over Convex Bodies for Learning Optimal Regularizers
stat Machine Learning.summary:
We consider the question of describing gradient flows over the collection of convex bodies. This is motivated by foundational questions arising in inverse problems. Suppose we wish to solve an ill-posed inverse problem using regularization techniques. Can we learn an optimal choice of a convex regularizer directly from prior data? Given a numerical algorithm that computes such an optimal regularizer, is there a principled manner for describing the evolution of its iterates? The objective of this paper is to lay the foundation towards answering these questions.
  To this end, we consider a criterion of an optimal regularizer based on seeking a convex body that minimizes the expected gauge evaluation with respect to a prior data distribution subject to a volume constraint. The formulation is initially nonconvex, but admits hidden convexity by passing to its polar. We characterize the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions that certify global optimality. We also analyze the $L^2$-gradient flow as well as a minimizing movement scheme with the Hausdorff penalty. Our results show that the objective gap decays exponentially along the gradient flow and we obtain dimension-dependent rates for both the objective gap and distance to the optimal body for the Hausdorff scheme. Finally, we apply the KKT conditions to identify explicit optimal convex bodies. For data where the optimal nonconvex regularizer is the $\ell_p$-quasinorm, $p \in (0,1)$, the optimal convex regularizer is the volume-normalized $\ell_1$-ball. For data described by paired basis atoms, the optimal convex regularizer is the polar of a shifted zonotope.

Computation.title: Combinatorial Bernoulli Factories with Polynomially Many Coins
Computation.summary: We provide an efficient implementation of combinatorial Bernoulli factories. Such a factory turns coins of unknown biases $x$ into a random vertex of a polytope $P$ whose mean is exactly $x$. For every affine slice of the cube (the class of polytopes that admit a factory), we give a single algorithm whose expected number of coin flips and running time at every interior $x$ are polynomial in the dimension and in $1/{δ_*}$, where ${δ_*}=\min_i\{x_i,1-x_i\}$ is never supplied to the algorithm. For perfect matchings this gives $O(n^{8}{δ_*}^{-2}\log(n/{δ_*}))$ flips, while the factory of Niazadeh, Paes Leme, and Schneider [STOC 2021] spends at least $n^{2n-1}$ flips in expectation at the uniform doubly stochastic matrix. For other polytopes, our method rounds exactly given a point deep inside $P$ and the promise that $x$ is far from the boundary of $P$.

Computation.title: GraphInfer: Statistical Inference for Decomposable Graphical Models in R
Computation.summary: Decomposable graphical models combine closed-form maximum likelihood estimation with local model comparison, which makes structure inference practical with many variables. The R package GraphInfer provides one likelihood framework for decomposable models of continuous, discrete and mixed data, the last as conditional Gaussian models. Structure inference ranges from exact minimum forests and stepwise search to stochastic global search. Nested models are compared by likelihood-ratio tests whose null distributions are exact in finite samples: conditionally on the discrete data for edges with a continuous endpoint, and conditionally on the discrete margins of the smaller model for edges between discrete variables. Missing values are handled by EM, by structural EM, which reuses complete-data searches through a weighted pseudo-sample of expected sufficient statistics, and by multiple imputation; selected models are fit to the observed-data likelihood. The package also treats the graphical models induced by irreversible event accumulation on trees: a search over the compatible graphs whose tree moves overcome an obstruction to single-edge moves, fitting of the full accumulation model with measurement noise and bootstrap tests of the accumulation hypothesis. GraphInfer is an independent, pure R successor to the archived package gRapHD. The implementation is validated against independent references, and simulation studies inform its defaults.
Computation.comment: 44 pages, 2 figures, 15 tables. The R package GraphInfer 0.1.0 will be submitted to CRAN; until then, the package and the replication material are available from the author on request

Computation.title: Sticky Manifold Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo for Bayesian Model Averaging
Computation.summary: Assigning positive prior probability to lower-dimensional submodels enriches the range of uncertainty that Bayesian models can represent. The resulting posterior distributions combine continuous parameter uncertainty with discrete model uncertainty. Efficient movement between these submodels, however, can be difficult to design. We propose the sticky manifold construction as a principled, modular framework for combining piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) across different submodels. The integration is rejection-free, requires no additional likelihood evaluations, and retains the non-reversible and ballistic nature of the component PDMP dynamics. We prove that the resulting process leaves the intended mixed-dimensional target invariant. We also develop a manifold PDMP algorithm based on coordinate charts to provide the within-submodel dynamics and a blow-up procedure that resolves singular sets into codimension-one sticky boundaries. This geometric construction makes the remaining design choices explicit; component dynamics and unsticking kernels can be chosen freely, subject to easily verifiable velocity compatibility conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the sticky manifold algorithms in Bayesian model averaging examples, propagating uncertainty over pure versus mixed states in quantum state tomography, rank in Bayesian principal component analysis, and parametric families in survival extrapolation.

Computation.title: A perturbation theory for Feynman-Kac models and their particle interpretations
Computation.summary: We develop a perturbation analysis of Feynman--Kac models, describing how local errors introduced at each step of the Feynman--Kac recursion propagate over time. Under general conditions on the potential functions and the Markov transitions, which are shown to hold for a large class of state-space models, we prove that the global error for any time horizon $T\geq 1$ is bounded by $C\,Δ_T\log(1+Δ_T^{-1})$, where $Δ_T$ is the largest local error; this bound holds both for the prediction and the updated models. These conditions require no Lyapunov function and no stability of the Markov transitions, and allow for non-compact state spaces: confinement is provided by the potential functions. Our perturbation bounds hold in total variation and in the Kolmogorov norm; for the latter, we extend the Hardy--Krause variation and the Koksma--Hlawka inequality to unbounded domains. Our perturbation theory is applied to derive time-uniform bounds for linearized Kalman filters, Euler schemes for partially observed diffusions and nudged state-space models, as well as high-probability error bounds, uniform over whole trajectories, for particle filters and, more generally, for mean field particle methods such as sequential Monte Carlo and diffusion Monte Carlo algorithms.

Computation.title: Scentree: a framework for generating scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming
Computation.summary: We present scentree, an open-source Python package for constructing scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming models using either historical data or samples drawn from a probability distribution. It combines machine learning and multivariate time series models to obtain a scenario fan that captures dependencies in the stochastic processes. This scenario fan is subsequently reduced into a scenario tree that preserves representativeness of the stochastic process, providing a flexible and extensible framework for uncertainty modeling in stochastic programming problems. The framework can also be naturally applied to two-stage stochastic programming problems. Key contributions are the joint modeling of the stochastic process, preserving correlations between all random variables, and the automation of the complete workflow, including forecasting model selection, parameter estimation, scenario fan generation, and scenario tree construction. In addition, scentree does not assume any underlying data distribution, reducing the statistical expertise required to produce a scenario tree, and is modular by design, allowing external forecasts and other partial executions of the workflow.

Computation.title: AIDA: Analysis of Interval Data in R
Computation.summary: AIDA is an R package that provides tools for the analysis of interval-valued data, including construction, visualization, robust estimation, and explainable outlier detection. The package is built around the intData class and is designed to support methodological research and applied workflows involving interval-valued data. AIDA implements methods for symbolic covariance estimation based on the Mallows distance, robust estimation via the Interval Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator, and explainable outlier detection using Shapley values. The package also includes visualization tools to support interpretation of the results and several interval-valued datasets.

Computation.title: Estimation and Inference for Multiplicative Error Models via Analytical Derivatives
Computation.summary: Maximum Likelihood Estimates (MLEs) of the parameters of a Multiplicative Error Model are typically computed through a standard gradient method, an iterative procedure usually based on numerical approximations to derivatives of the log-likelihood function, owing to the complexity of the analytical derivatives, which involve recursive terms. Building on previous work developed mainly in the GARCH framework, we derive analytical expressions for the score vector and the Hessian matrix of the Multiplicative Error Model log-likelihood by adopting the Gamma distribution for estimation purposes. Then, we illustrate how the iterative algorithm based on the analytical derivatives should be computationally implemented. After maximizing the log-likelihood, we also provide explicit formulas for several estimators of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the MLE. Additionally, we provide analytic formulas for robust covariance estimators that remain valid under distributional misspecification, which are also referred to as the asymptotic variance of the Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimator. We also propose a covariance estimator that is consistent under general forms of heteroskedasticity of the error term, while the usually adopted estimators rely on a specific variance assumption. The finite-sample performance of the covariance estimators is assessed through a Monte Carlo investigation. An application on real data completes the analysis.

Computation.title: R Package iglm: Regression under Interference in Connected Populations
Computation.summary: We introduce R package iglm, which implements a unifying regression framework for studying relationships among binary, count-, and real-valued predictors and outcomes in connected populations with interference due to spillover, contagion, and other complex phenomena. On the computational side, the regression framework provides scalable methods that can be applied to small and large data sets, by solving a convex optimization program based on pseudo-likelihoods via accelerated Minorization-Maximization algorithms. On the statistical side, the regression framework comes with provable theoretical guarantees for statistical estimators, including consistency results and rates of convergence for maximum pseudo-likelihood estimators. To increase the versatility of iglm, users can add custom-built model terms. We showcase iglm using data on hate speech on the social media platform X and communications among students.

Information Retrieval.title: REWEAVE: Online Learning for Workload-Adaptive HNSW Indexes
Information Retrieval.summary:
Vector databases rely on Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) indexes for similarity search, but a graph built from data alone can be poorly matched to a skewed or changing query workload. We present REWEAVE (Reward-Guided Rewiring of Vector Graphs), an online index-maintenance method that learns edge utility from query feedback and periodically rewires the bottom layer within the original per-node degree cap. The method supports sparse exact-neighbor feedback combined with self-labels, and standard HNSW serving without learning overhead once adaptation is disabled.
  Under explicit assumptions we prove value-estimation and graph-stabilization guarantees. Under stationary skew, REWEAVE improves held-out recall by up to 23.3 percentage points over HNSW. In comparisons with query-aware baselines on up to 100M vectors, it achieves up to 3.3x NGFix's query throughput at recall@100 of 0.80. On Amazon-ESCI with query drift, it increases stream recall@100 from 0.745 to 0.979 with 34% fewer search distance computations than frozen HNSW. These results illustrate the potential to improve retrieval quality and reduce search effort within an existing graph-degree budget, while incurring additional work during adaptation.
Information Retrieval.comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Full version with appendix

Information Retrieval.title: Wayfinder: Adaptive Resource Routing from Agent Citations
Information Retrieval.summary: To act effectively, agents must gather contextual information across resources such as chats, issue trackers, email and knowledge bases, to answer questions like "what was decided in the last project meeting?" or "where is the FAQ for our internal tooling?" Where this information lives in a user's environment is unknown to the agent, so it re-explores the same resources across consecutive interactions. Common routing approaches represent each resource as a tool and rely on high-level descriptions to generalize to unseen environments. Such descriptions often fail to separate similar or overlapping resources and cannot improve from the agent's subsequent interactions. We introduce Wayfinder, an adaptive router that uses the documents cited by the downstream agent as feedback about where relevant information resides. These citations update Wayfinder's internal resource representations, which subsequent interactions use to prioritize the resources likely to contain relevant information. We also introduce resource augmentation during offline reinforcement learning, which anonymizes and permutes resource identities to discourage training-time overfitting of which resource holds which topic; our ablations suggest it helps most when few training environments are available. Because no openly available professional environments pair realistic queries with resource-access patterns, we construct and release three controlled testbeds derived from existing datasets: NFCorpus, FEVER and Tech Startup. Compared with supervised, tool-retrieval and contextual bandit baselines under a shared closed-loop protocol, Wayfinder gives the best routing when resources contain semantically overlapping content that static descriptions cannot distinguish, while description-based tool retrieval suffices when resources are drawn from distinct corpora.
Information Retrieval.comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 10 tables. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026

Information Retrieval.title: Predicting the Needle in a Petabyte Scale Haystack: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation in Satellite Imagery
Information Retrieval.summary: Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: https://github.com/ShreelekhaR/predicting-the-needle
Information Retrieval.comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, to be published in NeurIPS 2026

Information Retrieval.title: Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search with Recall Guarantees Using Graph Spanners
Information Retrieval.summary: Graph-based indexes such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs make nearest-neighbor retrieval efficient, but a high average recall can hide queries whose results fall below an application's quality requirement. We introduce Certify-then-Rectify (CTR), which returns an initial graph-search result when a calibrated rule accepts it and searches for missing neighbors otherwise. The recovery search reuses the existing graph and the distances already evaluated by the initial search. To determine how far this search should proceed, we relate metric distances to graph-path lengths through graph stretch. We develop Stretch-Bounded Expansion from Query (SBE-Q), together with Metric Bound Verification (MBV) to prune unnecessary work, and estimate its budget from paths to the fraction of true neighbors needed for the requested recall. Finite-sample tolerance bounds support this recall-aligned estimate; paths recorded during proposal recovery offer a conservative alternative to separate shortest-path computations. Independent tests certify initial acceptance and recovery outcomes, giving an end-to-end population recall guarantee even when the estimated stretch does not cover every relevant path. If recovery cannot be certified, rejected queries use exact scan. Experiments on HNSW compare five stretch estimators, assess recovery efficiency, and evaluate compliance and throughput on databases of up to 100 million vectors. CTR is not specific to HNSW, and we also evaluate it on another graph index.

Information Retrieval.title: HeriKGQA: Grounded Knowledge-Graph Question Answering over Cultural Heritage Sensor Data
Information Retrieval.summary: Cultural heritage sites are increasingly monitored by sensor networks, but querying their data requires database expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural-language interface, yet over raw sensor records they lose track of which sensor, site, and time each value belongs to, and silently miscompute. We present HeriKGQA, a knowledge-graph question-answering method that confines the LLM to interpreting questions and phrasing answers, leaving computation to SPARQL and deterministic code. Questions are parsed into intents constrained by a heritage ontology aligning W3C SOSA/SSN with CIDOC-CRM, compiled into SPARQL, and answered from query results and temporal, spatial, and anomaly facts derived by a grounding layer, with error correction guarding each LLM step. On 500 questions over real data from five heritage sites, HeriKGQA reaches 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM and receiving the same anomaly rules and answer conventions, with comparable answer quality while running almost four times faster. Without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points and on anomaly questions from 99% to 66%. We report lessons from development and live deployment.

Information Retrieval.title: Bag of concepts can enhance other text representations for medical systematic review screening
Information Retrieval.summary: The paper examines the choice of text representation for semi-automated systematic literature review (SLR) systems based on active learning. Motivated by the insufficient attention that the bag of concepts representation has received so far, the paper discusses the implementation and experimental evaluation of several variations thereof. The experimental study was performed on medical SLR case studies, with results reported for random forest classification, cluster initialization and uncertainty sampling. The utility of bag of concepts features obtained using different ontologies is evaluated by applying them within the active learning framework to sequentially create classification models based on training data iteratively expanded with expert annotations. Systematic experiments compare BoW, BoC, PubMedBERT, Jina, Gemma and Qwen3 representations, together with combinations of BoC and each of the other representations. The evaluation uses workload savings and performance profiles adapted from optimization benchmarking. The results suggest that concept-based features can provide complementary information, with the BoC-augmented representations achieving higher mean workload savings on the DERP cases than their corresponding base representations. The Qwen3+BoC representation gives the best average performance in this comparison. The effects of augmentation vary across case studies and base representations. The paper also concentrates on the impact of ontology choice on document classification outcomes. In particular, the paper compares the predictive value of bag of concepts representations based on chosen ontologies with that of representations obtained using MedCAT with a UMLS-based dictionary.

Information Retrieval.title: When Local Definitions Are Missing: Stable Errors in Language Models
Information Retrieval.summary: Contracts, technical manuals, and online communities often give familiar words special meanings and define them in one place. A language model that reads a passage without that definition may use the usual meaning and give an answer that sounds right but is wrong. We study this with multiple-choice questions whose correct answers depend on a local definition. The questions come from a synthetic vocabulary, commercial contracts, Reddit community glossaries, and the documentation of a decentralized exchange. We ask three language models each question with and without the definition. Without using the answer key, we then test whether their repeated answers and stated confidence reveal their own errors. Separately, we give a small open model the answer key and test whether it can predict which questions larger models get wrong. We report three findings. (1) Familiar words that a source redefines cause the most errors. Models often repeat the same wrong answer, and neither repeated answers nor stated confidence reliably flag it. (2) The source definition fixes most errors on synthetic questions, but a definition drawn from the model's own prior knowledge does not. In real contracts, the source definition fixes only about half of the errors. (3) Given an answer key, a small model can rank questions by how likely larger models are to get them wrong. These results call for tests that check answers against the full source, including its local definitions.

Information Retrieval.title: When Does Low-Bit Quantization Preserve the Decisions of Vector Search?
Information Retrieval.summary: An orthogonal rotation improves the distance rank correlation of two-bit Cohere codes from 0.75 to 0.91, yet increases nearest-neighbour comparison flips by 51%. We analyse quantization through the comparisons made by graph search. A comparison changes only when its quantization error exceeds its exact margin, giving a flip bound that separates close calls from large errors. Shared endpoints induce correlated distance errors that partly cancel within a comparison. An exact replay identity connects candidate-level actions to the output of neighbour selection. A Gaussian model gives coordinate-code errors in closed form, and a rare-spike construction exposes heavy tails in the population-radius error. Held-out blocks give model-free certificates for acceptance rules based on exact or quantized margins. Across 24 dataset-code configurations, calibration-estimated risk correlates with held-out ranking and pruning flips at 0.97 and 0.99, compared with 0.91 and 0.99 for a margin-to-noise summary and 0.74 and 0.05 for distance rank correlation. Paired builds of 200,000-vector graphs connect rotation, query scoring, and topology to end-to-end recall and search work.
Information Retrieval.comment: 51 pages, 5 figures; substantially revised with expanded theory, calibration controls, and graph-search experiments

Information Retrieval.title: The Oracle and The Prism: A Decoupled and Efficient Framework for Generative Recommendation Explanation
Information Retrieval.summary:
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into explainable recommendation systems often leads to a performance-efficiency trade-off in end-to-end architectures, where joint optimization of ranking and explanation can result in suboptimal compromises. To resolve this, we propose Prism, a novel decoupled framework that rigorously separates the recommendation process into a dedicated ranking stage and an explanation generation stage. This decomposition ensures that each component is optimized for its specific objective, eliminating inherent conflicts in coupled models.
  Inspired by knowledge distillation, Prism leverages a powerful, instruction-following teacher LLM (FLAN-T5-XXL) as an Oracle to produce high-fidelity explanatory knowledge. A compact, fine-tuned student model (BART-Base), the Prism, then specializes in synthesizing this knowledge into personalized explanations. Our extensive experiments on benchmark datasets reveal a key finding: the distillation process not only transfers knowledge but also acts as a noise filter. Our 140M-parameter Prism model significantly outperforms its 11B-parameter teacher in human evaluations of faithfulness and personalization, demonstrating an emergent ability to correct hallucinations present in the teacher's outputs. While achieving a 24x speedup and a 10x reduction in memory consumption, our analysis validates that decoupling, coupled with targeted distillation, provides an efficient and effective pathway to high-quality, and perhaps more importantly, trustworthy explainable recommendation.
Information Retrieval.comment: We have identified several issues in the paper

Information Retrieval.title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
Information Retrieval.summary: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/DISL-Lab/RetailBridge.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted to KDD 2027 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (Cycle 1)

Information Retrieval.title: ReAlign: Reward-Guided Preference Alignment for Generative Re-Ranking
Information Retrieval.summary: Re-ranking refines the upstream ranked list to maximize listwise user utility. Existing two-stage generator-evaluator methods decouple list generation from list evaluation, leaving the generator without direct access to the listwise utility signal, while scoring-based one-stage methods score items under a fixed upstream permutation context without explicitly searching the permutation space. We propose \textbf{ReAlign}, a reward-guided preference alignment framework that couples a listwise reward model with a candidate-aware autoregressive generator. The reward model decomposes the listwise reward into position-wise contributions, modeling user exposure through a survival-based exposure module and item value through per-objective heads for heterogeneous engagement signals. The generator is trained in two stages: supervised pre-training on logged exposure lists to establish a relevance prior, followed by reward-guided post-training that aligns the generator with the reward model through complementary distribution and ranking alignment over within-pool standardized rewards. Extensive offline experiments show that ReAlign consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

Information Retrieval.title: SurvEval: Listwise Re-Ranking Evaluator via Survival-Based Exposure and Multi-Objective Value Modeling
Information Retrieval.summary: Re-ranking is a crucial stage in recommender systems, yet existing evaluators oversimplify user browsing assumptions and collapse multi-objective signals into a single scalar, limiting their ability to reflect true listwise utility. We propose \textbf{SurvEval}, a listwise evaluator that jointly models user exposure and item value for re-ranking evaluation. We formalize the sequential browsing process as a discrete-time survival model, deriving monotonically decreasing reaching probabilities that capture the cascading structure of user browsing. We further introduce a multi-objective value estimation module with dedicated per-objective prediction heads and uncertainty-based loss weighting to adaptively balance objectives of varying scales and noise levels. Both components are jointly optimized via a unified transformer backbone, and the listwise utility is obtained by summing the position-wise products of reaching probabilities and conditional item value estimates. Extensive experiments on KuaiRand and Avito demonstrate that SurvEval achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines.

Information Retrieval.title: SimRec: Learning to Search, Ask, and Recommend from Simulated Interaction
Information Retrieval.summary: LLM-based recommendation agents can search catalogs, inspect products, ask users, and revise rejected recommendations. However, these behaviors are often governed by hand-designed workflows, while existing training methods optimize isolated components such as query rewriting or list ranking rather than the interaction policy as a whole. We present SimRec, a reinforcement learning framework that trains the full interaction policy of a tool-integrated recommendation agent. SimRec introduces two components. A task-anchored user simulator provides feedback on every recommendation: conditioned on the current task need rather than on user profile, and it can be an external LLM or the recommender itself under self-play. A task-aligned reward optimizes the whole trajectory with GRPO, crediting natural retrieval quality and valid tool use alongside the final hit, with training-only target injection to handle sparse hits over large catalogs. On ESCI and Amazon C4, SimRec improves the NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% and from 22.94% to 24.72%}, outperforming training-free agents on far larger backbones and task-aligned baselines on NDCG. Analysis shows that the trained agent verifies candidates, uses preferences, and recovers from rejected recommendations far more often than its untrained counterpart. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/SimRec .

Information Retrieval.title: When Direction Matters: Diagnosing Relational Instruction Following in Dense Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Dense retrievers increasingly claim the ability to condition retrieval on natural-language relevance criteria beyond a short query. We identify a specific weakness in this capability: the evaluated models perform well when lexical or attribute cues distinguish the target, but become much less reliable when relevance depends on a directional relation over the same entities. We introduce SwitchIR, a controlled diagnostic that contrasts Constraint Shift and Explicit Filtering with Relational Flip, where the query and document pair remain fixed while the requested relation direction reverses. Across representative embedding and late-interaction retrievers, the primary joint metric is high on the two cue-available controls and consistently low on Relational Flip; the same ordering persists in an LLM-assisted, manually reviewed realistic variant. An exact margin decomposition shows that both directions are correct only when the direction-sensitive query--document interaction exceeds the direction-invariant pair preference. Empirically, direction-sensitive changes are common, but their aligned interaction is usually too weak to overcome that preference. Diagnostic fine-tuning shows that models can learn relational behavior that generalizes across relation families, with stronger generalization in the larger model.

Information Retrieval.title: What Score Distillation Transfers to Compact Dense Retrievers
Information Retrieval.summary: Compact retrievers are often specialized by distilling a large embedding model's similarity scores on hard negatives mined by the teacher model. We argue that this common setup calls for a different loss than the scale-dependent ones usually used, such as MarginMSE and PairMSE. When the teacher discards candidates scored too close to the labeled positive, the negatives it keeps get nearly identical scores. These losses then mostly ask the student to reproduce this tiny score range rather than the teacher's ranking. A per-row Pearson correlation loss, invariant to the shift and scale of the scores in each row (a query and its 32 candidates), avoids this failure, and removing PairMSE's scale term alone recovers most of Pearson's lead. We propose row scale dispersion, computed from the untrained student before training, to tell when this matters. With this loss, on rows mined around a labeled document, the teacher's scores substitute for relevance labels rather than add to them. Training on the binary label alone works as well, with the same loss or, for one student, a contrastive loss: the teacher's value lies in choosing the negatives. Without labels, the teacher's scores on its own top-ranked documents recover most of the labeled gain, largely through its top document as a pseudo-label. Experiments with two compact students on three BEIR datasets support both conclusions, including, for one student, comparisons with MarginMSE and a tuned listwise KL. We suggest a simple practical rule: distill teacher-mined negatives with a scale-free loss and, on such rows, use the teacher's scores where labels are missing rather than on top of them.

Information Retrieval.title: Vision-Grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment for Scalable Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval (TBPR) aims to retrieve individuals with texts in multiple languages. Despite its practical importance, it has been overlooked by existing research, which mainly focuses on English-only retrieval. The only prior attempt at multilingual TBPR suffers from (1) the absence of a large-scale, multilingual pretraining dataset and (2) a suboptimal model architecture for multilingual text encoding and cross-modal alignment, which employs a shared encoder that overlooks linguistic heterogeneity and relies on English as a pivot for cross-modal alignment, introducing English-centric bias. For this, we contribute MultiPedes, the first large-scale, pedestrian-centric multilingual pretraining dataset. It contains 10 million image-text pairs across four languages, constructed by a multilingual quality-aware data construction pipeline. We also propose ViSeLA (Vision-grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment), a novel framework featuring: (1) a semantic-aware multilingual learning module that extends the mixture-of-experts architecture by routing language-invariant semantics to specialized experts for improved multilingual feature learning; and (2) a vision-grounded cross-modal alignment module that employs a semantic probe to capture fine-grained semantics across modalities, enabling direct cross-modal alignment without relying on a pivot language. Extensive experiments on both multilingual and English-only TBPR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ViSeLA. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Flame-Chasers/ViSeLA

Information Retrieval.title: Measuring, Revealing and Mitigating Harmful Content Propagation in Recommender Systems
Information Retrieval.summary: Recommender systems help users navigate vast amounts of information by filtering content according to their historical behaviors. As these systems increasingly shape everyday information access, they largely determine the content users are exposed to. However, current research typically prioritizes catering to user interest, while overlooking the existence and propagation of harmful content, such as violence, hate speech, and pornography. In this work, we take a systematic step toward investigating harmful content in recommender systems from three aspects: measuring, revealing, and mitigating. First, we construct datasets with harmfulness-related annotations and present new evaluation metrics to quantitatively measure the harmfulness of recommendation results. Second, our empirical analysis reveals that users tend to engage with harmful content and prevailing recommendation methods often contribute to the proliferation of such content. Third, to address this issue, we introduce a generic framework, MitiHarm, which integrates harmfulness-related signals into both item and user representation learning. Experiments show that MitiHarm can significantly mitigate the propagation of harmful content while preserving user satisfaction. Resources of this work are available at https://github.com/Zhang-xiaokun/MitiHarm.

Information Retrieval.title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
Information Retrieval.summary: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations. Despite its importance, curiosity is hardly incorporated into modern recommender systems for lack of a formal measure. The information-gap theory of curiosity provides no formal quantitative model that a recommender system can operate on, and existing proxy metrics do not accurately measure the curiosity that a recommended item evokes. To fill this research gap, we formalize the information-gap theory into five axioms of curiosity and construct the canonical formulation of a computational measure of the curiosity that a recommended item evokes in a consumer. We validate our curiosity measure through a survey-based study, in which it matches consumers' self-reported curiosity and outperforms alternative proxy metrics. We subsequently build a curiosity-aware recommender system that incorporates this measure into the utility function design, and we show through offline experiments on three real-world datasets that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.

stat Machine Learning.title: There Will Be a Scientific Theory of Deep Learning
stat Machine Learning.summary:
In this paper, we make the case that a scientific theory of deep learning is emerging. By this we mean a theory which characterizes important properties and statistics of the training process, hidden representations, final weights, and performance of neural networks. We pull together major strands of ongoing research in deep learning theory and identify five growing bodies of work that point toward such a theory: (a) solvable idealized settings that provide intuition for learning dynamics in realistic systems; (b) tractable limits that reveal insights into fundamental learning phenomena; (c) simple mathematical laws that capture important macroscopic observables; (d) theories of hyperparameters that disentangle them from the rest of the training process, leaving simpler systems behind; and (e) universal behaviors shared across systems and settings which clarify which phenomena call for explanation.
  Taken together, these bodies of work share certain broad traits: they are concerned with the dynamics of the training process; they primarily seek to describe coarse aggregate statistics; and they emphasize falsifiable quantitative predictions. We argue that the emerging theory is best thought of as a mechanics of the learning process, and suggest the name learning mechanics. We discuss the relationship between this mechanics perspective and other approaches for building a theory of deep learning, including the statistical and information-theoretic perspectives. In particular, we anticipate a symbiotic relationship between learning mechanics and mechanistic interpretability.
  We also review and address common arguments that fundamental theory will not be possible or is not important. We conclude with a portrait of important open directions in learning mechanics and advice for beginners. We host further introductory materials, perspectives, and open questions at learningmechanics.pub.

stat Machine Learning.title: A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration
stat Machine Learning.summary: We study smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, which measures how far a sequence of probabilistic forecasts is from being calibrated and, unlike the classical expected calibration error, is robust to small perturbations of the forecasts. Against adaptive adversaries, the minimax smooth calibration error is known to lie between $Ω(T^{1/3})$ and $O(\sqrt{T})$ (Qiao and Zheng, 2024), where $T$ is the number of rounds. In this paper, we close this gap by constructing a new adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual. This design makes compensating for past residuals costly, and forces every forecaster to incur an expected smooth calibration error of $Ω(\sqrt{T})$. This lower bound matches the known upper bound up to universal constants, and further implies $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. Overall, our results settle the minimax rates of these calibration measures in sequential prediction. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.

stat Machine Learning.title: Your PID Is Already a Neural Network: Learning Its Gains with Only Three Weights and No Teacher
stat Machine Learning.summary: A discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent neural network, a classical state-space fact: a fixed linear memory of the running integral and the last error, read out by three trainable weights that map one-to-one to the PID gains. Networks with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs of any width, only approximate it. Trained only on a one-step physical cost (the expected cost of one transition from a fixed state distribution), with no demonstrations, teacher controller, or known gains, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem, so gradient descent converges from any initialization to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; the limit network is that PID, with the same action on every error sequence. Partitioned regression then shows what extra capacity buys. Orthogonal residual features keep these gains and improve on the PID if and only if they correlate with the part of the optimal action outside the PID span. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap is 5.88% of the optimal PID cost, and 4.00% against PID with a bias; no controller can improve on PID by more on this objective. A residual started at a tuned PID begins exactly at that PID; at the one-step optimal PID, a fixed-feature residual's first gradient step lowers the cost if and only if its features can improve on the PID. Experiments confirm the realization, recovery, and gap results to numerical precision. On held-out plants of three families, under a protocol frozen before the test data existed, a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID and trained with it lowers the long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5%, and 1.9%, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison with the PID tuned alone suggests that most of it comes from the recurrent part in two families. The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.
